**(A)** Biotic factor

The living components of an ecosystem, plants, animals and microorganisms, make up its biotic factors, which the chapter lists as plants, pathogens, parasites and predators in an organism's habitat. Abiotic factors are the non-living, physico-chemical ones such as temperature, water, light and soil. 'Direct' and 'indirect' are not the standard way of dividing the components of an ecosystem.

**(A)** Biotic community

The chapter defines a community as several populations of different species in a particular area that interact with one another. A population is made of individuals of the same species only, and an ecological niche is the functional role of one species, not a group of organisms. An ecosystem is wider than a community because it also includes the abiotic environment.

**(B)** Commensalism

The chapter gives the clown fish living among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone as an example of commensalism. The fish gains protection from predators, which keep away from the tentacles, while the anemone does not appear to gain or lose anything. In mutualism both partners would benefit, in parasitism one would be harmed, and in amensalism one is harmed while the other is unaffected.

**(D)** One species is benefited, other is harmed.

In parasitism the parasite benefits by living on or in the host and feeding on it, while the host is harmed: its survival, growth and reproduction are reduced. 'One species is benefited' alone does not say what happens to the other species, so it fits commensalism equally well. Benefit to both describes mutualism, and benefit to one with the other unaffected describes commensalism.

**(A)** exponential growth

A freshly inoculated agar plate holds a few bacteria and plenty of nutrients and space, so for the time being resources are effectively unlimited. Under such conditions, the chapter explains, a population realises its full potential and grows in an exponential (geometric) way. Logistic growth, which is the same thing as Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth, sets in only when resources become limiting, and zero growth would mean births and deaths cancel out.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; it does not discuss bacteria on an agar plate. Standard biology gives exponential growth for a population with unlimited resources, as on a newly inoculated plate.]
